They were lilies, the kind with the trumpet shapes, and if Biscuit had chewed even a piece of one leaf, she could not wait. That was her inference, and the only other idea, that a tiny bite might be harmless, did not seem plausible enough to risk.

Peyton put Biscuit in the bathroom with water and his towel, called the animal clinic, and then carried the whole bouquet out to the porch and set it on the railing. When her mom's car pulled in, Peyton was standing at the door holding the kitten. "We have to give Grandma's flowers away," she said. "I'll tell you on the way to the vet."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, Congress can override a president's veto if two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to pass the bill again.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen table had become the United States Congress, more or less. Rose had pushed the salt shaker to one side to be the White House, and the pepper grinder was the president, which everyone agreed it resembled. On Monday her class would hold a real simulation, with roles drawn from a hat, and Rose wanted to be ready for anything.

"Okay," she said. "Our bill to make recess five minutes longer passes both houses." Nikola, sprawled in Grandpa's recliner, raised his hand as the Senate. Uriah, representing the House, drummed on the table. "But the president vetoes it," Rose announced, and turned the pepper grinder around to face the wall. The bill went back to them, which was the part she kept forgetting, so she made herself say it out loud. "The president's veto is not the end. Congress can override a veto, but only if two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to pass the bill again." Two houses, two separate two-thirds. That was the rule. Uriah whistled.

They tried it with numbers. The House had twenty-six kids in the simulation, so Rose needed eighteen of them, and in the Senate, with twelve kids, she needed eight. She wrote each total on a napkin and taped the napkins to the pepper grinder, in case the pepper grinder forgot. Nikola, playing a senator who did not like recess on principle, voted no just to rebel, and Rose made him do the arithmetic anyway, because a no vote was a variable like any other vote. It counted against her two-thirds the same as a no from someone who truly hated swings.

Then came the crisis drill. Rose stacked the votes: seventeen in the House, one short. The bill died on the table while the pepper grinder looked smug, if a grinder could. "So it isn't enough to win," Uriah said slowly. "You have to win by a lot, in both places, or nothing happens." Rose slid the napkins off the grinder and pocketed them for Monday. From the doorway, Grandpa cleared his throat. "In my day," he said, "we lobbied with cookies." Rose looked up at the plate in his hands, then at Nikola. "You're a senator," she said. "How do you feel about oatmeal?"

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
The back of the moving truck smelled like cardboard and dust, and John sat between two tall stacks of boxes while the truck rumbled out of his old street. Most of the boxes had nothing on them except a scrawled "MISC" in his dad's marker. One box near the front, though, had neat writing on every side: "BATHROOM: towels, soap, toothbrush." John had written that one himself, because Mr. Huang next door had lent him the marker and asked what was in it.

John pulled out his phone and texted Muhammad, who had moved to a new town last spring. "What was the worst part of unpacking?" Muhammad answered fast: "First night I couldn't find my sheets. Slept in my jacket. Nobody knew which box was which." John looked down the truck. There were at least forty boxes, and the word MISC appeared on maybe thirty of them. If the sheets could be in any of those, finding them meant opening every single one, which sounded tedious enough to take all night.

He tried an experiment while the truck rattled on. He picked a MISC box, peeled it open, and looked inside: books, a lamp, and a rolled-up poster. He couldn't tell from the outside what was in there, and he couldn't tell from the inside which room it belonged in, because the stuff had come from three different rooms. He taped the box shut again and exhaled, then inhaled slowly, the way he did before a swim race.

"We should write on them," he called up to his dad through the little window behind the cab. "Every box gets the room it goes in and what's inside." His dad said fine, if John did the writing, and pulled over at a gas station so they could reach the stacks safely. For the next hour, John opened lids, peeked, and marked boxes: "KITCHEN: pots," "JOHN'S ROOM: sheets and blankets," "GARAGE: tools." The last one had half a peanut butter sandwich in it, and Muhammad, riding along to say goodbye, said the microbes on that thing were probably building a city by now. John threw it out the door into the trash can and wrote "GARAGE: board games" on the box.

When they reached the new house after dark, the truck's back door rolled up and John read the labels out loud. His dad carried "KITCHEN" boxes straight into the kitchen, and John grabbed the one marked "JOHN'S ROOM: sheets and blankets" and walked it up the stairs. Muhammad leaned in the doorway, watching.

"Told you," Muhammad said. "First night, sheets."

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: A cut whose edges gape open may need stitches, skin glue or closure strips from a doctor or nurse to heal well.
story:
Nolan had assumed first aid would be mostly bandages, and bandages were tedious, so he was halfway asleep in Mr. Alvarez's garage, where the babysitting course met on Saturdays. Then Aida, who was supposed to be practicing on the rubber arm, dropped the coffee tin full of broken glass they used for the "hazard station," and a shard caught her thumb on the way down.

"Bleeding," Aida announced, sounding more curious than scared. "Actual bleeding. On day one."

Cecelia shoved the hazard tin behind the lawn mower while Nolan grabbed the practice kit. He pressed the gauze on, waited, then peeled it back to look. The cut was clean but deep, and its edges sat apart like two lips refusing to speak to each other. Every time he drew the bandage tight, the edges pulled apart again, and a bead of blood welled up between them. He tried a second bandage crossing the first, then a third going the other way. The gap yawned under all of them.

"That's not working," Cecelia said.

"It's hinging open," Nolan said, watching the edges swing apart each time Aida bent her thumb. He thought about the garage door, about how a door only stays shut if the latch catches both sides. A bandage was a weak latch. He looked at Aida. "I think this one's past us. Grabbing Ms. Ferreira."

Ms. Ferreira, next door, took one look and said, "Gaping like that, it may need stitches, or skin glue, or closure strips from someone at the clinic to heal properly." She drove them, and a nurse painted the cut shut with glue that stung, then sealed it with little strips like tiny white staples.

Back in the garage, Nolan taped a note to the practice kit: bandage for closed cuts, doctor for open ones. Then he picked up the coffee tin and set it, gently, on the highest shelf.

"Day one," Aida said, holding up her glued thumb like a trophy.

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Many plant cells have one large central vacuole, a water-filled sac that can take up most of the cell, while animal cells have only small vacuoles, if any.
story:
Alyssa had rewritten her cell diagram three times, and the giant blob in the middle still looked wrong. Ms. Grant had set the task for Friday: build a model comparing a plant cell and an animal cell, and name the parts only plants have. Alyssa wanted hers to be the best in the class, but she couldn't figure out what that huge bubble in her plant cell drawing was supposed to be. The animal cell next to it had no such bubble at all, which made her wonder if she had copied something wrong.

She cornered Carys at the lunch table, where Carys was already sketching a plan to make her cells out of cake. "If I frost it, the whole class will remember mine," Carys said, turning her notebook so Alyssa could see. "What's this giant circle filling your plant cell?" Alyssa asked, tapping her own diagram. Carys squinted. "Maybe a mistake? My book has it too, though."

At the back of the room, Scott was taping labels to his foam ball model, muttering the parts like a chant. Chloroplasts, cell wall, chloroplasts, cell wall. Alyssa noticed he had skipped the bubble entirely. "Why'd you leave that out?" she asked. "Because it's clearly not a real part," Scott said. "Nothing takes up that much of a cell. It'd squash everything else." That made Alyssa pause. Was there really a sac big enough to fill most of a cell? And if so, why would an animal cell exclude it?

She decided to test it. If the bubble was real, then a plant cell soaked in water should behave differently from an animal one, since a water-filled sac would swell. She asked Ms. Grant for two slides, a thin slice of onion skin and a scraping from her own cheek, and set them side by side under the microscope. Through the lens, the onion cells looked like bricks, each with a dark mass pressed against the wall. Her cheek cells were pale blobs, no big central anything inside them, just small scattered dots.

"There," she said, half to herself. "The onion has one big sac. Mine doesn't. So Scott's model is missing a part, and it's a real one." Scott leaned over, looked, and groaned. "It's called a vacuole," Alyssa read from her textbook, "and plant cells get one big one. Animal cells only have small ones, if they get any at all." Scott pulled the tape off his foam ball and started carving out the middle with a scissors.

By Friday, Alyssa's poster showed both cells in molten-looking wax, red for animal, green for plant, with the giant vacuole glowing like a water balloon in the middle of the green one. Carys's cake had a lime jelly center that wobbled when she carried it in, and the whole class leaned forward when she cut it. Ms. Grant held up Alyssa's label card, which read, "Parts only plants have: cell wall, chloroplasts, and the big central vacuole." Scott raised his hand first. "Can I borrow the wax for the makeup quiz?"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Layla's right shoulder had started to ache somewhere deep, in a place she couldn't point to exactly. She had done sixty jump serves, maybe seventy, because Coach kept saying her serve was the only weapon the team had. Across the gym, Emrik was pitching into a net for the baseball team that shared the space on Thursdays, and his coach had just called out, "That's your limit, Emrik. Sixty pitches. Done for the day."

Layla stopped mid-motion, ball balanced on her palm. "Why sixty?" she asked him later, when they were both at the water fountain. "You don't even look tired."

"Coach says growth plates," Emrik said, rubbing his elbow. "Areas of growing cartilage near the ends of our bones. They're weaker than the bone around them, so young athletes get limits on repetitive stress." He shrugged like it was unfair, a small rebellion against being told to stop, but he said it like a rule he'd memorized.

Repetitive stress. Layla walked back to the serving line turning the words over. Sixty serves, then another ten, then another ten, all vigorous, all on the same arm, landing in the same sore spot that had been quietly aching for two weeks. Her shoulder hadn't gotten worse from any single hit. It was deteriorating a little at a time, from the same motion repeated, exactly the kind of thing limits were for. She remembered the previous Saturday, when she'd served until the lights went off and told herself the ache was nothing. Maybe that choice had been the wrong one.

She tested it, the only way she could. She served ten left-handed, clumsy things that barely cleared the net, and her right shoulder rested completely, no twinge, no pull. Then she took ten easy underhand serves with her right arm, gentle ones, and felt the difference at once: no sharp pinch. The problem wasn't serving. It was hammering the same spot without a count, without a limit.

Coach came over with the ball cart. "You've got the strongest arm on this team, Layla. Another fifty before we lock up?"

She looked at the clock, then at her shoulder, as if it might answer for her.

"Twenty," she said. "Twenty, and I'm writing down every one."

Coach tilted her head, then nodded slowly and handed her the ball.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
Adam had saved nine dollars for the mangoes, the big golden ones stacked near the front of Sun Fresh Market. Last week they had cost two dollars each, but a storm had wrecked the harvest somewhere far away, and now the sign read four dollars. He counted the pile: only eleven mangoes sat in the bin, and he watched a woman pick one up, turn it over, and put it back. "Too much," she muttered to no one, and walked toward the apples, which filled a whole row of crates and cost half as much.

Adam wanted mangoes for Friday, when his grandmother came to visit, because she was frail lately and mangoes were the one thing she always said tasted like home. He looked from the nearly empty bin to the towering apple crates, then to the oranges, piled in a loose tsunami of color that rolled right to the edge of the shelf. The oranges were cheap, and people kept grabbing bags of them. Every cart that passed him seemed to hold oranges or apples. Almost nobody carried a mango.

He tested his idea the way he tested things in science class, by watching. When a worker wheeled out a cart of bruised mangoes and marked them down to one dollar, three shoppers crowded around at once and the bin was bare in four minutes. High price, few buyers. Low price, many buyers. He thought of his friend Ellie's lemonade stand last summer, when she had doubled her price and half her customers had walked past. "It works the same every time," Adam said under his breath.

Ellie herself appeared at the end of the aisle, hunting for snacks. "What are you staring at?" she asked.

"Prices. When the price of something goes up, people buy less of it. When it goes down, they buy more. Watch." He pointed at the mango bin, empty except for one last fruit.

Ellie watched a man scoop a dozen cheap oranges into a bag and nod. "Huh. So what are you going to do about your grandma?"

Adam picked up the final mango, turned it over, and set it gently back down for the grandmother part of Friday, then carried a bag of oranges to the register and counted out his change.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
The waiting room clock said 3:20, and Everley's birthday party started at four. Madison sat with her left arm propped on a pillow, a bag of ice sweating on top of it, and did the math again. Twenty minutes to be seen, twenty minutes for X-rays, twenty for the doctor. She might make it. She might not.

She had been climbing the fence behind Mr. Campbell's garage, showing off a new move, when her hand slipped and she came down hard on the pavement. Mr. Campbell had driven her here himself, holding the door and saying, "Steady now," in the same voice he used for nervous dogs. The pain had climbed for a while and then leveled off, like a hill that reaches a plateau and goes flat, a steady dull ache that she could almost ignore.

The X-ray technician clipped the films to a light box outside the exam room, and while the nurse went to find the doctor, Madison stood in the hallway and studied them. Two pale shadows ran side by side through her forearm, and she could see the break, a hairline crack in one of them. But which one? She wiggled her thumb, then her little finger, watching each move travel down toward the crack. The thumb side. The crack was on the thumb side.

When the doctor came around the corner, Madison pointed at the film. "Is that the radius?"

He stopped, surprised. "The radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side," he said. "Yes, that's your radius."

Everley arrived at 3:50, out of breath, holding a purple marker. The doctor wrapped the cast quickly, and while it was still fresh, Everley wrote HAPPY BIRTHDAY TO ME across it in looping letters.

"There's a sign at the nurse's station about flammable liquids," Everley said, capping the marker. "So no birthday candles near that thing."

"Tell that to your cake," Madison said, and held out her good hand for the party invitation.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
Louis had one question written on the folded note in his pocket, and he intended to get an answer before the bus left the nature reserve. The class had hiked past the wetland in the morning, where vapor rose off the warm water in thin curls, and after lunch Mr. Dlamini led them to the paddock beside the visitor centre, where three cows grazed behind the fence.

"They nominate one kid per group to sketch the animals," Sullivan said, holding up his clipboard. He wanted his sketch chosen for the display board at school, so he had been drawing all day. He looked at the nearest cow, a big brown one, and frowned. "Mine keeps stopping. How am I supposed to draw it if it won't hold still?"

Louis watched the cow too. Its head was up, its mouth empty, yet its jaw swung side to side in slow circles. It wasn't eating anything new. He unfolded his note, which he had written to himself before the trip: cows eat grass, so why chew with no grass? He had an idea, and a way to test it. He crouched at the fence and waited for the cow's jaw to stop. When it did, the cow lowered its head, tore a mouthful of tough grass, and swallowed it almost whole. Louis counted seconds. One minute passed. Then the jaw started its circles again, with nothing in the mouth.

"It swallowed," Louis told Dante, who was timing on his watch. "Then it chewed later. So the food comes back up." Dante scribbled it down. At the station inside the centre there was a model of a cow cut open in cross-section, with four separate pockets stacked inside. Louis found a small brass label on the first pocket. "Rumen," he read aloud. The card beside it said the rumen held microbes, tiny living things that helped break down tough grass, and that the cow later brought that grass back up and chewed it again as cud.

"So it chews twice," Dante said. "Once for real and once later." Sullivan was already redrawing his cow, jaw mid-circle, with a small arrow and the word cud printed neatly underneath. story:
Emmett stood at the kitchen counter with a crumpled flyer from Mr. Goldberg's class spread in front of him. The assignment said to explain supply and demand using strawberry prices, and it was due tomorrow. His problem was simple: he did not understand it yet.

"Think about last summer," his mom said, chopping carrots behind him. She had a memory for everything. "That farm stand by the lake. You ate two baskets before we paid."

Emmett remembered more than the eating. He remembered the farmer at closing time, calling out a lower and lower price, almost begging people to take her berries. He had presumed she was just being generous. Now he turned that memory over, looking at it from a different angle. What if she had no choice? He pulled a notepad closer and tested the idea out loud. "Strawberries go bad in days. You can't save them for later. If you're stuck with too many, you have to cut the price or lose them all."

His little sister wandered in, notorious for sneaking snacks, and stopped at the word strawberries. "Are there any?"

"Not here," Emmett said. "That's the whole point. In winter there are barely any, so they cost a lot. In summer there are tons, and they're cheap, because they can't be stored."

Then a message arrived on the tablet from his classmate Valerie: "Still stuck on the strawberry thing? My dad won't drive us to the farm stand so I can't check prices. Ask your mom about the winter ones." Emmett typed back: "Winter ones come from far away and there aren't many. Summer ones are everywhere and they spoil within days, so growers dump them cheap." Valerie replied with a thumbs-up and one line: "Mr. Goldberg will never believe I got it from you."

Emmett hesitated, thumb over the screen. Part of him wanted to point out that he had figured it out alone, in his own kitchen, and that Valerie had done nothing but message him at nine at night. Another part remembered all the times she had shared her notes when he was sick. He typed "anytime" and set the tablet down, still not sure that was the fair answer. Then he picked up his pencil and wrote his first sentence.

fact: Seedlings grown indoors are usually hardened off, set outside for a little longer each day, so they can adjust to sun and wind before planting.
story:
Blake had been dreading this moment all morning: the moment he would have to tell his grandpa that the tomato seedlings were dead. He had grown them from seed on the windowsill in the kitchen, tall and green, and yesterday he had carried them out to the garden bed behind the shed and planted every one. This morning they lay flat against the soil, pale and wilted, as if the sun had flattened them on purpose.

His grandpa knelt beside the bed and touched a drooping stem. "They were pampered," he said. "Windowsill plants have to be hardened off first. Set outside for a little longer each day, so they can adjust to sun and wind before planting." Blake stared at the row of failures and thought about yesterday, how proud and vain he had been, showing off his seedlings to the neighbour over the fence. He had rushed everything. He remembered skipping his own garden guild meeting to plant them, certain he already knew more than the other kids.

That afternoon he wrote a letter to Kelsey, who ran the guild's tomato project.

"Dear Kelsey, I planted my indoor seedlings straight into the garden and they wilted. Grandpa says they needed to adjust to sun and wind first, a little longer outside each day. Do you have any seedlings left? I still have seeds, but I don't want to wait a month. Blake."

Kelsey's reply came tucked in his grandpa's mailbox two days later. "I have six seedlings. But you have to promise to harden them off. One hour outside the first day, then longer each day. No shortcuts." Blake read it twice, then carried the letter out to the porch, where his grandpa sat shelling peas. "Can I borrow a tray?" Blake asked. "I'm going to do it right this time." His grandpa handed him a wooden flat and said, "Hour one starts now," and pointed at a bright patch of sun by the step.
